title: 🔥 Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437)
rawNotionMarkup: Newly authored, creator-authorized working canon — 21 November 2026. This reference expands the cultures, states, communities and politics of the Era of Fire, the THIRD ERA of the SECOND AGE, Years 1,322–1,437 inclusive (116 years). It builds on the previously established exiled dark mages, their magical creation of the southeastern Avarran Southern Wastes and volcano at the beginning, and the world-shaking earthquakes that ended the age. All lore is revisable at the creator's discretion. A historical polity named below is not automatically an ancestor, founding dynasty, or earlier form of any present-day kingdom. ## The century after Wonder The Era of Wonder left many regions prosperous, scholarly and proficient in new lunar magics born of moon fragments. The Era of Fire did not instantly extinguish that prosperity across the planet. Its hallmark was a sharper contest over what people should do with hard-won power: safeguard it, regulate it, sell it, wield it, or abandon it. A failed harvest in one valley could coexist with a rich university city across the sea. A royal court could condemn an unfamiliar spell while employing a mage to keep its wells flowing. Because the Era lasted only 116 years, many long-lived Khazari and Eldar who had experienced the Era of Wonder personally also saw the Era of Fire begin and end. Human, Goblin, Halfling, Ogre and other shorter-lived households experienced it across generations. No universal character, birth-rate change, compulsory profession or common religion is assigned to an entire people. The name “Era of Fire” has several later explanations—forge fires, hearths guarded during crisis, burned farmland, and fearful stories about magic—but no single definitive etymology is established. Its name should not be reduced to the southeastern volcano alone. ## I. Avarra — the wound in the southeast and the kingdoms beyond ### The Ashward Flight — the people of the former farmlands At the very opening of the Era, Year 1,322, the already-established bands of exiled dark mages united in southeastern Avarra. They created both the Southern Wastes and their volcano with dark magic, destroying the region's prior character as fertile farming country. The land's destruction was deliberate. It did not result from the worldwide earthquakes, which came 116 years later. A new tradition remembered as the Ashward Flight traces some of the displaced farming households that fled beyond the altered land's margin. It is a collective name for many movements, not one single column, army, prophecy, or established total of survivors. Their descendants preserved seed names, irrigation songs, livestock marks, family recipes and competing accounts of which village paths had been lost. Some people could carry little more than relatives and tools; others reached markets with wagons, deeds and surviving grain. Who escaped, who stayed, and the full human cost remain unknown. One set of later refugee and market records is called the Ashward Registers. Different receiving communities recorded names, debts, orphaned kin, seed loans and disputed land claims rather than a reliable full census. A family's place in such a register does not establish the lost homeland's royal dynasty or the identities and species of the exiled mages. Boundary: The dark mages made no treaties, alliances, trade arrangements or diplomatic relationships with outside peoples. The Ashward Flight concerns the devastation and others' responses; it is not a history of contact or diplomacy with the mages. ### The Crown of Three Fords — a regional human river kingdom A substantial but now-vanished human-ruled river kingdom in western/south-central Avarra is remembered as the Crown of Three Fords. Its lands encompassed floodplain farms, bridge tolls, independent market charters and smaller Halfling, Goblin and other communities with differing civic rights. Its rulers' real strength was the administration of waterways and grain reserves rather than an army able to overrun an entire continent. During the Era of Fire, the Crown developed the Bread Oath: a royal relief duty by which participating ford towns kept public stores for travelers and displaced families during scarcity. Some officials honored the rule; others demanded impossible proof of residence, charged predatory tolls or favored powerful estates. A notable reforming monarch, Queen Merea of the Three Fords, supported court appeals against officials who confiscated grain from displaced households. Local landlords and merchants resisted her policies, and she never achieved uniform justice throughout her lands. These events are new regional history; the Crown is not declared identical with Aldermere, Valtoria, a current republic, or an earlier government of Karak-Varn. Whether any modern families preserve authentic descent from its ruling house remains open. The kingdom's final dissolution and exact lifespan are not dated here. ### Khazari — the Hearth-Gate Agreements Several independent mountain halls and engineering polities in and around old Ironspine negotiated what later craft histories call the Hearth-Gate Agreements. A participating hall promised that important passage gates, communal ovens, water channels and emergency shelters would remain physically inspectable and operable when a rune behaved unexpectedly. This extended the earlier Two-Hand Rule without abandoning Runecraft, Deepcraft, Forgebinding or other distinct Khazari disciplines. The agreements were disputed. Some prestigious rune-houses considered the inspections an insult to proven craft; some stonewrights accused wealthy magical guilds of gambling with workers' lives. Settlements disagreed over who paid for spare parts, who might be admitted to shelters, and whether a guild's expertise should outweigh a foreman's field observation. A celebrated disagreement, the Debate of the Two Keys, concerned whether an engineer could close a dangerous gate without a runesmith's consent. Different halls adopted different answers. Do not claim these halls were the already-established modern Seven Mountain Thrones, or that the agreements founded the modern Deepways, royal dynasties or First Throne institutions. Ironspine itself existed long before the First Age; the era did not create it. ### Eldar — the Grove-Court of Seralith In parts of the broad western woodland, a regional Eldar grove-court, remembered as Seralith, maintained living seed archives, water gardens and networks of skilled healers. The court's public ideal was custodianship without monopoly: knowledge of endangered plants should be preserved, but whether it should be freely shared with neighboring farms became a bitter controversy. Some wardens opened their gardens to outsiders. Others insisted that a woodland community, threatened by logging and a changing magical world, had the right to keep rare seed and restorative arts to itself. The court staged an annual Vigil of Two Flames: one flame kindled by ordinary means, the other maintained by a permitted magical working, both tended by volunteers. Their coexistence symbolized the lesson that practical labor and magic need not be enemies. It was a Seralith custom, not an universal Eldar religious rite, and it was not a newly invented cosmic magical source. Seralith is not automatically the modern Eldar High Sovereignty, a named living royal dynasty or the sole ancient court of Letharion. ## II. Tharvorn — winter politics and roads of rescue Northern communities across Tharvorn encountered a different Era of Fire. The most consequential local fires were often literal hearth fires and beacon signals: essential to navigation, winter rescue, drying food and keeping mountain roads from vanishing into storms. In some valleys, long-valued enchantments worked well; in others, dangerous overconfidence in them prompted practical reforms. The Frost-Hearth Confederation was a temporary alliance of several independent cold-country settlements and smaller lordships, not the present Northern Holds. It coordinated rescue shelters, winter trail markers and stores of fuel and fodder. A hall that refused a traveler shelter without adequate reason could lose the right to draw from shared stores. Wealthier members sometimes resisted feeding poor or transient households, so confederation meetings could be openly contentious. Human winter-keepers, Wolvenkin guides, Bearfolk households, some Giant and Troll neighbors, and coastal Merfolk observers all contributed through different local arrangements rather than serving a single people. Some Giant families refused centralized agreements and maintained independent refuge sites; some Troll river-keepers became renowned for safe ice crossings but disagreed with confederation officials about tolls. No whole species is cast as a servant, monster, or uniformly heroic participant. The Red-Lantern Custom grew in participating northern ports: a steady lamp signaled safe shore, while a patterned sequence signaled a landing made dangerous by shifting ice or shallow water. Its practical use outlasted its precise original codes in some communities. ## III. Sahrad — the Blue-Jar Crown and water as law In Sahrad, a regional kingdom known in surviving Second Age accounts as the Blue-Jar Crown governed a cluster of river-fed agricultural towns and adjoining dry-country routes. It was one of several powers, not a retroactively named Southern Sultanate and not the ruler of the entire continent. Its signature institution was the Jar Hearing. When villages disputed a canal or reservoir, each side was required to present records of water drawn, crops planted and repairs performed; ceramic jar seals made tampering more difficult. Skilled human surveyors, Elephantfolk stewards, Centaur caravan representatives and other local neighbors might serve in the proceedings, but access was far from equal: some rural communities were underrepresented and powerful households could still bend the rules. The Dispute of the Seventh Gate became famous as a public argument over whether water for a distant market's livestock could be diverted from established farms in a hard season. An eventual compromise combined timed access, emergency cisterns and labor obligations. It solved one regional dispute rather than inventing an all-continent water law. Sahrad also maintained highly varied port, savanna, river and desert cultures. Along some trade corridors, Goblin factors and Gnome wellwrights gained reputations for careful measurement, while others preferred performance, scholarship, farming or soldiering. None of these jobs is a biological obligation. The Blue-Jar Crown's precise founding date, last ruler and connection (if any) to modern human houses remain unwritten. ## IV. Orundel — the Reed-Crown League and the War of Three Locks On riverine parts of Orundel, several autonomous ports and river principalities formed the Reed-Crown League. Members traded flood forecasts, recognized one another's merchant weights and maintained embankments. Some leaders were hereditary princes, others council-elected magistrates, and some towns held mixed-species assemblies in which membership and privilege were fiercely contested. This was not a single kingdom uniting all Orundel. In the middle portion of the Era of Fire, rival participants fought a limited, regional conflict remembered as the War of Three Locks, a struggle over controlled river passages, tolls and irrigation. It involved river flotillas, sieges of waterworks and arguments over who possessed lawful authority to open floodgates. The war did not involve Orcs, exiled Southern Wastes mages or the First Throne, and it is not assigned to the separate older east–west war traditions. Several seasons of disrupted shipping eventually led to mediated gate-access agreements; later towns disputed which side had truly won. No fabricated world-scale casualty total or global conquest follows from it. In coastal and forest settlements beyond the League, Tigerfolk families, Gnomes, Humans, Centaurs, Goblins, Harpies, Merfolk and other peoples followed their own distinct livelihoods. River-bell circles coordinated flood warnings in some mixed communities. A bell sequence could signal a washed-out crossing without relying on unstable magical signals; it was engineering and communal practice, not a universal supernatural gift. ## V. Vaelora — the Lantern Orchard Councils In Vaelora, lake and old-forest settlements developed a loose network remembered as the Lantern Orchard Councils. These were assemblies of distinct communities rather than a throne or continent-wide empire. Their most successful work was coordinating the rebuilding of storm-damaged bridges, exchanging medicinal cuttings and sheltering traveling families when routes became unsafe. Eldar, Halfling, Gnome, Foxfolk, Human and other households participated where locally present, with different rules of representation. The most persistent dispute concerned who held the right to take a cutting from an old tree. Some guardians treated it as public medicine; others believed removing a rare branch endangered sacred groves. The Orchard Reconciliation was a limited agreement among participating towns to appoint local keepers and record gifts, not a ruling on the ethics of every Eldar or Aelwyn court. Stories of the Hushed Groves record places where Ent neighbors and woodland keepers requested silence, seasonal restraint or protection from careless cutting. Some traders respected these requests, while others dismissed them as burdensome. Aelwyn Fae courts, where involved in local stories, retained their own meanings and promises; they are not the same people as Pixies, Brownies or Eldar. ## VI. The many peoples of the Era Goblins: Several contemporary Second Age records describe Goblin orcharders, road merchants, clerks, marsh pilots and repair families. The Copper-Thread Caravans were a loose network of mixed Goblin-led trading households that specialized in keeping credit and weights intelligible across different local laws. They were not a kingdom, military caste, or universal Goblin culture. Some families settled permanently at crossroads; some traveled seasonally. Their story predates the Orcs' creation, and no Goblin–Orc alliance can be placed in this Age. Ogres: In scattered regions some Ogre communities operated farms, quarry yards, timber haulage, river barges, independent lodges and roadside inns. The Great Road Suppers were customary gatherings in a handful of working communities, where road laborers and neighbors brought meals and negotiated the next season's public works. An Ogre stonemason, Braghal of the Wide Bridge, appears in one surviving regional tale as the principal designer of a crossing used by mixed traffic. This is an individual's achievement, not evidence that all Ogres were builders or that Ogres and Orcs share an established biological origin. Halflings and Gnomes: Some Halfling boroughs wrote hearth claims for families uprooted by local disasters, reserving access to land and tools without forcing them into a particular lord's hereditary service. Different boroughs made very different choices. Gnome waterworks, lantern artisans and instrument makers developed independent testing practices, but Gnome magic remained its own cultural tradition and was not rewritten as Khazari Runecraft. Centaurs and Merfolk: Some steppe and savanna Centaur communities negotiated migration passage and grazing rights with farming neighbors; some Merfolk communities maintained coastal hazard memories, water conditions and safe landing knowledge. They had their own histories of conflict and cooperation, not merely supporting roles in human ports. Ents, Aelwyn and other unusual peoples: Some surviving Second Age histories describe woodland compacts and seasonal rites associated with Ent communities and independent Aelwyn traditions. They must not be merged with all fairy folk. Where a different currently recognized people is not securely placed in this Age, do not invent a species-wide origin date from this chapter. Small peoples and animal peoples can have local histories without making the entire world or every culture identical. Dragons, Giants and Living Mountains: Their exact involvement in these specific 116 years is not determined by the appearance of their names in later legends. No confirmed dragon war, Living Mountain awakening, or Giant-founded global dynasty is added here. Local Giant settlements and personalities may be present without resolving the mysteries of Living Mountains. ## VII. Magical ethics, worship and the politics of fear Mage law was uneven. Some cities created trial licenses for dangerous workings, others trusted guild examination, and a few courts imposed cruel restrictions on innocent practitioners because they feared the dark-mage disaster far away. The Hearth and Witness movement in several unrelated communities argued that a spell's benefit must be witnessed, its risks disclosed, and its failure survivable. Some leaders genuinely protected their neighbors; some used the language of safety to enrich their own institutions. Nothing in these debates erases the real distinction among intrinsically good, grey and evil magical forces. The exiles accessed dark magic; that does not establish that every form of Shadowcraft, every independent mage, or any particular people is inherently evil. Lunar magic still originates in the moons; Eryndor independently produces Natural Magic or the World's Breath. There is no newly invented source moon or named god responsible for the Southern Wastes. The First Age's destroyed lunar magics remain permanently lost. New moon-fragment-derived forces and surviving older traditions could still be studied and used. Priests, practical engineers, learned mages, skeptical workers and ordinary worshippers developed conflicting interpretations. No universal anti-magic law, religious conversion, or revelation about a specific deity was imposed worldwide. ## VIII. The final years and the breaking of the Second Age During the Era's final generations, the institutions above could prosper or decline on their own terms. The cause of the eventual planetwide earthquakes is not assigned to the mages, regional wars, lunar magic, divine anger, a known kingdom or the First Throne. In Second Age Year 1,437 the established globe-shaking earthquakes ended the Second Age. Far-western Avarran lowlands and marsh country were raised violently into new mountains; the pre-existing Ironspine's deep roots amplified aftershocks tenfold across Eryndor. Large numbers died, settlements and cultures could be devastated, yet no entire species became extinct, in part through an as-yet-undetermined magical force. The specific deaths of the named rulers, destruction of the regional polities in this chapter, or universal survival of their records are not established. The dark mages' volcano had already existed since Year 1,322. These earthquakes intensified it; the mages then restrained its potential devastation by harnessing its energy, unwittingly increasing their own power. The mages remained isolated from other peoples and their groups endured well into the Third Age. No Orcs existed before the Third Age. The same dark-mage groups created them sometime during that later Age, with an ambition to besiege Khazari strongholds and eventually attack Eldar and human kingdoms. The creation method, date and military outcomes remain open. ## IX. Historian's ledger — what is now established, and what is not - New working historical canon in this chapter: Ashward Flight and partial refugee records; the regional Crown of Three Fords and Bread Oath; Hearth-Gate Agreements and Debate of Two Keys; Grove-Court of Seralith and Vigil of Two Flames; Frost-Hearth Confederation and Red-Lantern Custom; Sahradi Blue-Jar Crown and Dispute of the Seventh Gate; Orundel Reed-Crown League and regional War of Three Locks; Vaeloran Lantern Orchard Councils; Copper-Thread Caravans; the Great Road Suppers and regional tale of Braghal; and varied local regulation of magic. - Unassigned on purpose: Exact maps/borders, census and army figures, court genealogies and royal succession beyond named individuals, formation/disbandment dates of these polities, any connection of new polities to modern states, full death tolls, definitive etymology of “Era of Fire,” specific missing Age-boundary victims, actual magical mechanism of the earthquakes, First Throne involvement, named gods and moons, unknown species origins, the Third Age creation method of Orcs, and the later fate of the dark mages. - Evidence limits: No authentic First Age records survive anywhere in known Eryndor. Records from the Second Age may survive, be copied, disputed or lost; their completeness is not guaranteed. The Era of Fire's events are creator-level world history and do not mean Gloin Hammerfeld knows them in the Fifth Age. His scene remains paused in the Royal Historical Archive in Karak-Varn on Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847 of the Era of Crowns, at approximately 11:25 AM. Cross-references: 03 — History & Ancient Lore; 02 — Peoples & Cultures; 04 — Magic & the Cosmos. ## Era names are continent-specific — historical naming canon (21 November 2026) CREATOR-ESTABLISHED RULE: Era names are continent-specific, not universal names used by every people across Eryndor. The names we have established for the Second Age — Era of Awakening, Era of Wonder and Era of Fire — are the Avarran historical names for those periods. Other continents — Tharvorn, Sahrad, Orundel and Vaelora — may have different names for their own historical eras, reflecting their respective experiences, cultures and traditions. Even within a continent, peoples and kingdoms need not all use identical terminology or calendars. Ages versus eras: The worldwide Ages are the common event-delimited chronological framework; locally named eras are ways that continents and cultures describe history within those Ages. Second Age: 1,437 years remains fixed. Avarra's established three-part Second Age division is Awakening (Years 1–321), Wonder (Years 322–1,321), Fire (Years 1,322–1,437) in retrospective Second-Age dating. These dates provide a historian's cross-reference for describing events elsewhere, not proof that other continents used those names, drew the same internal boundaries or divided their own histories into exactly three eras. No alternative names or boundaries are approved yet; do not invent them and present them as established. Third Age: The 8,873-year length and nine eras are the creator's proposed Avarran Third Age framework, not nine universally named eras shared by every continent. The duration and ninefold plan remain a working proposal as previously recorded. Other continents' era names, number of subdivisions and transitions are still open. Read all previous chapter headings accordingly: When an event in Sahrad, Tharvorn, Orundel or Vaelora is described as occurring during the “Era of Fire,” that label identifies the same date span using Avarran retrospective chronology; it does not make “Era of Fire” the local name used by inhabitants there. The names and descriptions of local historical periods await later creator decisions. The distinction does not alter established historical events, world-Age transitions, the exiled dark mages, the Third Age emergence of Orcs, or Gloin Hammerfeld's paused campaign.
